\title{What the index of substitution saturation measures,\\
       and why its critical value is a power threshold}

% =====================================================================
\begin{abstract}
\noindent
The index of substitution saturation $\Iss=\Hbar/\HFSS$
\citep{xia2003iss} is used to decide, before any tree is built, whether an
alignment retains phylogenetic signal. We show that the entropy construction
enters $\E[\Iss]$ only through the spectrum of the rate matrix: resolving the
transition matrix on the eigenbasis of the symmetrised generator
$S=\Pi^{1/2}Q\Pi^{-1/2}$ reduces the index to a linear functional of the
coordinates $\xi_\mu=\langle e^{\mu d}\rangle$, and $\Iss$ is an affine
function of the mean pairwise $p$-distance precisely when
$\tau_\mu/w_\mu$ is constant across the distinct non-zero eigenvalues of $Q$
($\tau_\mu$ the algebraic multiplicity, $w_\mu=\tr(\Pi P_\mu)$, $P_\mu$ the
spectral projector). The criterion holds for every reversible model under
uniform base frequencies --- where the affine relation is exact --- and for
every composition when the spectrum is degenerate; for non-uniform composition
with a non-degenerate spectrum, $\Iss$ retains one further coordinate, a
composition-weighted term that peaks at intermediate divergence. Whether the criterion holds or not,
$\Iss$ reads nothing about the number of substitutions actually realised
beyond what the uncorrected proportion of differing sites already carries, and
therefore inherits that quantity's saturation. The critical value fails for
reasons unrelated to the spectrum. Being per-site, $\Iss$ is intensive, its
distribution invariant to sequence length to $O(L^{-1})$, whereas $\Issc$
increases with $L$, so that the associated test statistic grows as
$\sqrt{L}$: significance becomes a statement about how many sites were
sequenced. In the near-saturated region the index is pinned within a few
percent of its upper bound, so its critical value is nearly invariant not only
to rate heterogeneity but to arbitrary changes in the underlying divergence ---
apparent robustness that is an artefact of boundedness rather than a
calibration. A four-taxon transfer of long branches at fixed patristic total
illustrates the consequence: $\Iss$ is constant along the path to $O(r)$,
while the probability of recovering the true topology spans nearly its full
range. Passing the test remains evidence against saturation; failing it is
weak evidence.
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction}

The index of substitution saturation, $\Iss=\Hbar/\HFSS$, was introduced by
\citet{xia2003iss} to answer a question that substitution models address only
implicitly: have a set of sequences accumulated so many multiple substitutions
that their phylogenetic signal is exhausted? Its construction is deliberately
minimal. $\Hbar$ is the mean entropy of the base composition at a site,
$\HFSS$ the entropy expected under full saturation, so the ratio requires only
an alignment --- no tree, no model fit, no likelihood. That independence is why
it is used: $\Iss$ can be computed before any phylogeny is built, and compared
against a tabulated critical value $\Issc$ to decide in advance whether a data
set is fit for analysis \citep{xia2003iss,xia2009handbook}.

The two halves of the test are constructed differently, and the difference
matters. The index itself is a statistic of the alignment; the critical value
is a threshold calibrated by simulation under specified conditions
\citep{xia2003iss}. Here we characterise the first exactly, and show that the
second fails for reasons that have nothing to do with that characterisation.

We show that the entropy construction enters $\E[\Iss]$ only through the
spectrum of the rate matrix, which reduces the question of what $\Iss$ measures
to a spectral one. Resolving the transition matrix on the eigenbasis of the
symmetrised generator $S=\Pi^{1/2}Q\Pi^{-1/2}$ makes the index a linear
functional of the coordinates $\xi_\mu=\langle e^{\mu d}\rangle$, and singles
out the condition under which it collapses onto mean pairwise $p$-distance:
the ratio $\tau_\mu/w_\mu$ must be constant across the distinct non-zero
eigenvalues of $Q$. The condition is met for every reversible model under
uniform base frequencies and for every composition when the spectrum is
degenerate, and it fails --- mildly, by a term we quantify --- in the
regime used to calibrate $\Iss$. Where it holds, $\Iss$ and mean
$p$-distance induce the same ordering of alignments, so the content of the
test is carried entirely by the critical value. That value we show to be
$L$-dependent, so that the test statistic grows as $\sqrt{L}$, and in the
near-saturated region to be pinned close enough to the index's upper bound
that it cannot track the divergence it is meant to threshold.

% =====================================================================
\section{Results}

\subsection{The statistic and its normalisation}
\label{sec:setting}

Let $N$ sequences of length $L$ be related by a tree $\mathcal{T}$ with leaf
states generated by a reversible rate matrix $Q$ stationary with respect to
$\bpi$, normalised so that $-\sum_j\pi_jQ_{jj}=1$. Write
$\hat{\mathbf p}^{(i)}$ for the empirical state frequencies at site $i$,
$\hat p_j$ for their average over sites (the pooled frequencies), and
\begin{equation}
  H_i=h(\hat{\mathbf p}^{(i)}),\qquad h(\mathbf p)=-\sum_j p_j\ln p_j,\qquad
  \Hbar=\frac1L\sum_{i=1}^{L}H_i .
\end{equation}
The normalising constant admits two readings, and both are needed below:
\begin{equation}
  \HFSS^{(A)}=\E_{\mathbf n\sim\Mult(N,\hat{\mathbf p})}\bigl[h(\mathbf n/N)\bigr],
  \qquad \HFSS^{(B)}=h(\hat{\mathbf p}),
  \label{eq:conventions}
\end{equation}
convention $(A)$ being Xia's \citep{xia2003iss,xia2009handbook} and convention
$(B)$ the plug-in composition entropy. Since
$\HFSS^{(A)}=h(\hat{\mathbf p})-\frac{K-1}{2N}+O(N^{-2})$, the two are related
on any data set by
\begin{equation}
  \Iss^{(A)}=c\,\Iss^{(B)},\qquad
  c=\frac{h(\hat{\mathbf p})}{\HFSS^{(A)}},\qquad c\in(1,\,1.08]\ \text{for }N\ge16 .
  \label{eq:convention}
\end{equation}
The convention rescales the index but changes neither which of two alignments
is more saturated nor, as \S\ref{sec:criterion} shows, whether the affine
relation holds.

\subsection{Spectral resolution}

Throughout, $\Pi=\operatorname{diag}(\bpi)$ and
\begin{equation}
  S=\Pi^{1/2}Q\,\Pi^{-1/2}=U\Lambda U^{\!\top},\qquad
  \Lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda_1,\dots,\lambda_K),\quad
  0=\lambda_1>\lambda_2\ge\cdots\ge\lambda_K .
\end{equation}
Because $Q$ is reversible, $S$ is symmetric, so its eigenvectors are
orthonormal and the spectral projectors are orthogonal:
\begin{equation}
  P_\mu=\sum_{k:\lambda_k=\mu}u_ku_k^{\!\top},\qquad
  \tau_\mu=\tr P_\mu\in\{1,\dots,K-1\},\qquad
  w_\mu=\tr(\Pi P_\mu)=\sum_j\pi_j(P_\mu)_{jj}.
  \label{eq:projectors}
\end{equation}
\todo{State Lemma 9 (spectral resolution
$P_{ij}(t)=\pi_j+\sum_{k\ge2}A^{(k)}_{ij}e^{\lambda_kt}$) and Lemma 10, and
prove $\tau_\mu=$ algebraic multiplicity. Use the orthogonal projector
Eq.~\eqref{eq:projectors}, \emph{not} the Lagrange form
$P_\mu=\prod_{\nu\neq\mu}(S-\nu I)/(\mu-\nu)$: the latter is numerically
unusable for $K>4$ (at $K=20$ it returns $\sum_\mu\tau_\mu\approx34$ instead
of $19$, and $w_\mu$ errors of order $10^0$; the orthogonal form is exact).
Note that $K=4$ is the last state space for which the non-zero eigenvalues are
given by radicals (degree $K-1=3$, Cardano); the criterion itself does not
depend on radical solvability, only the explicit closed form does.}

All quantities of interest are linear functionals of the \emph{same} vector
$\bxi$ with $\xi_\mu=\langle e^{\mu d}\rangle$, averaged over leaf pairs and
rate classes:
\begin{equation}
  \Psi=\sum_{\mu\ne0}\tau_\mu\,\xi_\mu,\qquad
  \wp=\Bigl(1-\sum_j\pi_j^2\Bigr)-\sum_{\mu\ne0}w_\mu\,\xi_\mu,\qquad
  \Delta=\sum_{\mu\ne0}\Bigl(w_\mu-\tfrac{\tau_\mu}{K}\Bigr)\xi_\mu .
  \label{eq:scalars}
\end{equation}
Here $\wp$ is the mean pairwise $p$-distance and $\Psi=\langle\tr P\rangle-1$.

\begin{remark}[Second-order accuracy varies strongly with $N$]
\label{rem:accuracy}
At $N=4$ --- the size used for the simulations below --- the second-order
affine line deviates from the exact expectation by $0.02$--$0.07$, i.e.\ by
$3$--$11\%$ of the attainable range of the index, and the exact chord slope
over a representative interval is $0.84$ against the predicted $1.082$. The
affine identity is qualitatively robust and quantitatively poor at small $N$;
all numerical claims about it should be made at $N\ge16$ or computed exactly.
\end{remark}

\subsection{When the index collapses onto \texorpdfstring{$p$}{p}-distance}
\label{sec:criterion}

\todo{Part II Theorem 6 with Corollaries 6.1--6.3 and Lemma 11.
State the failure condition as $\Delta\not\propto\Psi$, not $\Delta\neq0$.}

\begin{corollary}[Uniform composition]
\label{cor:uniform}
If $\bpi$ is uniform then $\Pi=I/K$, hence $w_\mu=\tau_\mu/K$ for every
$\mu$ and $\tau_\mu/w_\mu=K$ identically --- for \emph{every} reversible $Q$,
every topology, every branch-length vector and every rate distribution. The
proof is one line and never mentions whether the spectrum is degenerate.
\end{corollary}

\begin{remark}[Scope of the collapse]
\label{rem:scope}
The one-line argument fails exactly when the $\Pi$-average on some non-trivial
eigenspace departs from the global mean $1/K$. Three qualifications must be
stated, and the third is the strongest.
\emph{(i)}~For nucleotides the departure is small but not zero: with
non-uniform composition and a non-degenerate spectrum the deviation of $\Iss$
from the $p$-distance prediction is $0.014$ (least-squares) to $0.022$ (chord),
which is $4\%$ to $44\%$ of the separation between the symmetrical and
asymmetrical critical values, depending on the number of taxa --- the figure is
\emph{not} a single number.
\emph{(ii)}~The criterion depends on the stationary composition of the
\emph{model}; a uniform-frequency model in any alphabet satisfies it. In
practice nucleotide compositions are close to uniform while amino-acid
compositions are not, so the collapse is a nucleotide-scale result.
\emph{(iii)}~The decomposition above is \emph{second order}, and it would be
wrong to read it as a general statement that everything $\Iss$ adds beyond
$p$-distance is composition. At second order $\E[\Iss]$ depends on
$\Var(\hat p_j)$ alone, hence only on pairwise identity
$\langle P_{jj}\rangle$; beyond second order it depends on third and fourth
moments of the site-pattern distribution, which pairwise identity does \emph{not}
determine. The site patterns carry structure that the mean mismatch proportion
cannot see --- for $K=4$ a $2\!:\!2$ site is parsimony-informative while a
$3\!:\!1$ site is not, and the two have different entropies. The magnitude of
this higher-order channel is measurable and is reported in
Section~\ref{sec:simulation}; whether it is phylogenetically informative rather
than merely compositional is a separate question, answered by testing
conditional independence:
\begin{equation}
  \Pr\bigl(Y \mid \bar p,\, \Iss\bigr)\quad\text{versus}\quad
  \Pr\bigl(Y \mid \bar p\bigr),
  \qquad Y\in\{\text{parsimony-informative fraction},\ \text{recovery}\}.
  \label{eq:condindep}
\end{equation}
That test, and not the correlation between the two statistics, is what
adjudicates redundancy.
\end{remark}

\subsection{The critical value depends on sequence length}

number of sites, not the degree of saturation.}

\section{Discussion}

The two halves of the test come apart. The index is an affine image of the mean
pairwise $p$-distance whenever the composition-weighted term in
Eq.~\eqref{eq:scalars} is proportional to the phylogenetic term --- exactly so
for uniform composition or a degenerate spectrum, approximately so for
nucleotides generally --- and it therefore reads nothing about the number of
substitutions actually realised that the uncorrected proportion of differing
sites does not already supply. Saturation, in its standard sense, \emph{is} the
gap between the observed difference and the true divergence; a quantity affine
in the former inherits the gap rather than seeing through it. The rate of loss
follows: the index resolves true divergence at the rate the uncorrected
distance does, exponentially under rate homogeneity and as a power law under
$\Gamma$-distributed rates.

The critical value, meanwhile, is $L$-dependent, so that significance is a
statement about how many sites were sequenced; and in the region where the test
is actually applied the index is close enough to its upper bound that the
threshold cannot distinguish moderate from severe saturation. The practical
consequence is asymmetric. Passing the test is evidence against saturation ---
the index would be near its ceiling if the data were saturated. Failing it is
weak evidence, and is not by itself grounds for discarding sites; the remedy
for insufficient resolution is more data or more taxa, not fewer sites.

\subsection{What the 2003 paper got right}
\label{sec:right}

The critique above should not obscure four things.

First, the problem was real: before 2003, saturation was assessed by plotting
transition/transversion ratios against distance, or by permutation and skewness
tests, both of which report signal in a data set containing two closely related
species and an arbitrary number of fully saturated ones --- a defect the paper
states explicitly, and attributes to the first three of the four approaches it
reviews (the fourth, \citet{steel1993confidence,steel1995frequency}, is faulted
on different grounds: clumsy beyond four taxa, parsimony-specific, undeveloped).
The 2003 paper's own entrance is that the fourth approach's diagnostics had not
been developed further; that assessment has aged well.

Second, and most durably, the paper's central observation is correct: sequences
fail to recover the true tree long before $\Iss$ reaches $1$, so the quantity of
interest is a critical value, not the full-saturation limit. That observation is
what motivated later work to re-estimate critical values by ROC analysis against
the number of taxa and sequence length
\citep{duchene2021saturation}. It should also be said that the critical tree
length is defined \emph{two different ways} in the original: for the symmetrical
topology it is the tree length at which $P_{\mathrm{true}}=0.95$, whereas for the
asymmetrical topology, where the maximum recovery probability need not reach
$1$, it is the tree length at which $P_{\mathrm{true}}$ falls to $95\%$ \emph{of
its own maximum}. The two are not comparable, and every departure below is
measured on the first; the tabulated asymmetrical values therefore carry an
additional, unquantified source of drift.

Third, the simulation grid --- F84, transition/transversion ratio from 1 to 10,
base frequencies from 0.1 to 0.9, 4 to 32 taxa, two extreme topologies, 100
replicates per point --- is a serious design for its time, and the paper reports
the grid it used, together with the finding that composition and
transition/transversion ratio are negligible relative to topology, taxon number
and sequence length.

Fourth, the discussion section does not ignore rate heterogeneity. It treats the
rates-across-sites and covarion models at length, notes that the test applies to
the $(1-P)$ fraction of sites, and states that assuming $P=0$ when $P>0$ makes
the test \emph{conservative}. That claim is correct --- invariable sites depress
$\bar H$, hence $\Iss$, hence the rate of rejection --- and it is the same
channel as the $+I$ under-detection noted in Section~\ref{sec:collapse}. The
defensible criticism is narrower than "heterogeneity was overlooked": the
numerical calibration of the critical value does not carry $\alpha$ as a
coordinate, even though the surrounding text acknowledges that it should.

The failures are of a different kind: a normalisation whose entropy form
implies more than the second-order expectation delivers, a calibration whose
conditions were not stated as conditions of use, and a threshold whose
behaviour is governed by sample size and by the proximity of the index to its
own ceiling. None of these makes the reasoning wrong; together they make the
verdict the index issues unsupported.

\subsection{Relation to other approaches}
\label{sec:related}

\todo{States as substance, not as defence: earlier warnings
\citep{verbruggen2007codium,letsch2011rrna} question the threshold while
accepting the index, whereas we characterise the index itself. Duch\^ene et al.
\citep{duchene2021saturation} operationalise saturation as long tree length and
re-estimate the threshold by regression on $\sqrt{\#\text{taxa}}$ and sequence
length; their empirical finding is the phenomenological shadow of
Corollary~8.1. A posteriori branch-level tests \citep{manuel2025satute} are a
different construction, and given a tree and a model saturation is identifiable
per branch; what is not identifiable is saturation before the tree is
committed to.}

\subsection{Open question}
\label{sec:open}

Whether the rate-heterogeneity mis-calibration bites in practice depends on
where real data place the critical point on the index curve, which is
measurable and to our knowledge unmeasured. Data sets whose indices cluster
near the ceiling are in the robust regime; those that do not are not.
